# Acquired Perforating Dermatosis

**Authors:** Sarra Harbaoui, Noureddine Litaiem

**Source:** StatPearls - StatPearls Publishing

## Abstract

Perforating dermatoses are a heterogeneous group characterized by a papulonodular rash with transepidermal elimination of dermal components. Traditionally, 4 classical forms of primary perforating dermatosis have been described, where the transepidermal elimination mechanism represents the hallmark of the disease: Kyrle disease, reactive perforating collagenosis, elastosis perforans serpiginosum, and perforating folliculitis. Elastosis perforans serpiginosum begins in childhood and characteristically presents with eliminating elastic fibers. Reactive perforating collagenosis also occurs during childhood with the expulsion of collagen fibers. In perforating folliculitis, the content of the follicle, with or without collagen or elastic fibers, gets eliminated. Finally, Kyrle disease presents with transepidermal elimination of abnormal keratin. However, there is some controversy in the literature considering the classification of Kyrle disease. While a few authors consider Kyrle disease to be an acquired form of perforating dermatosis, some define it as a variant of prurigo nodularis, representing the end-stage of excoriated folliculitis. The secondary form of this condition is acquired perforating dermatosis (APD). See Image. Acquired Perforating Dermatosis. The term was proposed by Rapini in 1989 to designate all the perforating dermatoses affecting adults with diabetes mellitus, chronic renal failure (CRF), and rarely, other systemic diseases, regardless of the eliminated dermal material. Commonly, patients with APD present with umbilicated papules and plaques with predilection sites that include the trunk and extremities. Although the pathogenesis of APD remains unclarified, some authors suggested that trauma and microvasculopathy may be the triggers of transepidermal elimination and degeneration of the collagen fibers.
